item.title: Save the Children officially warned by regulator over staff put at risk in Yemen
item.description:
Warning from Charity Commission for England and Wales concludes two-year investigation after death of Hisham al-Hakimi in October 2023

The international aid charity Save the Children has been issued with an official regulatory warning over management failures and misconduct that put staff at its Yemen office at serious risk.

The warning concluded a two-year investigation by the Charity Commission for England and Wales into the running of the office after the death of its safety and security director, Hisham Al-Hakimi, in October 2023 after he was detained by the Yemeni authorities.

item.title: US-Iran hostility sees oil prices rise and shares fall
item.description:
US-Iran hostility sees oil prices rise and shares fall

Oil prices rose and share prices dropped on Thursday as the bad blood between Iran and the US was aired at the UN General Assembly.

Brent crude prices moved back to above $100 a barrel as American and Iranian leaders exchanged barbs at the United Nations in New York.

On Wednesday US President Donald Trump welcomed his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping to Washington for a three-day visit that is likely to impact the war on Iran.

item.title: Yemenis seek safety in Djibouti as African migrants continue arriving in Yemen
item.description:
Yemenis seek safety in Djibouti as African migrants continue arriving in Yemen

Submitted by MEE correspondent on Thu, 09/24/2026 - 09:40
Recent escalation has forced more than 3,000 Yemeni refugees to flee to Djibouti, even as African migrants continue to move in
Yemen refugees arrive in Djibouti as intensified fighting drives displacement (Reuters/Abdourahim Arteh)
Off

Abdullah Mohammed, 37, is a Yemeni expatriate in Djibouti, where he first arrived in 2017 after losing his job with an oil company in Yemen.

He works in a clothing shop, which yields enough to provide a decent living for his six family members back home.

Djibouti has welcomed thousands of Yemenis who travelled in search of work in an easily accessible neighbouring country - unlike the Gulf states, which are virtually impossible to reach for Yemeni refugees or those who cannot afford high visa fees.

“When I first entered Djibouti, I travelled with neighbours, and no special preparation was needed since visas are granted upon arrival," Mohammed told Middle East Eye.

"Since then, I feel like I am in my own country; the authorities don’t hassle us or demand high fees for visa renewals and other requirements."

Thousands of Yemenis work in Djibouti, travelling back and forth smoothly by sea or air.

Since the conflict in Yemen re-escalated in September, however, an estimated 128,000 people have been newly displaced, adding to the 5.2 million internally displaced persons (IDPs) already living in displacement across the country.

According to UNHCR., 3,601 new arrivals from Yemen were recorded in Djibouti as of 18 September, seeking safety from the renewed fighting between the Houthis (Ansar Allah), Saudi Arabia and the Saudi-backed national government.

'Everyone should give based on what they have, as Islam teaches us. We should never judge or treat people based on their nationality'

- Yemeni restaurant owner

Djibouti has long been a primary destination for residents of Yemen’s Red Sea coast due to its proximity and its willingness to accept Yemenis upon arrival as refugees. In response to the recent surge, authorities in Djibouti called on humanitarian organisations to intervene and assist incoming Yemeni refugees.

This is not the first group to reach Djibouti. UNHCR confirmed that neighboring countries continue to host Yemeni refugees and asylum-seekers, including approximately 4,000 in Djibouti and 8,000 in Somalia.

The newly arrived Yemeni refugees landed at scattered points along the coast near Obock. They are currently staying in refugee camps under increasingly difficult humanitarian conditions.

Mohammed explained that the economic situation in Djibouti is no longer what it used to be, making it hard for new arrivals to secure work.

“Those refugees are in camps and cannot leave freely to seek employment. Even if they do, finding a job is difficult because many Yemenis here are already unemployed,” he said.

He expressed hope that wealthy Yemeni business owners living in Djibouti would step in to assist their compatriots in starting over or returning to Yemen.

“All of us have been impacted by the conflict in Yemen, but these are newly affected people. I hope our traders can help them, at least with basic necessities,” Mohammed added.

African migrants still arriving in Yemen

While Yemenis flee to Djibouti and thousands are already in Ethiopia, at the same time Ethiopian and Somali migrants continue to arrive in Yemen despite the recent escalation in conflict.

According to the International Organization for Migration (IOM), 11,397 migrants entered Yemen in August - a 17 percent decrease compared to the 13,687 tracked in July. The primary departure point remained Djibouti.

In 2025, a total of 110,144 migrants were recorded entering Yemen, 97 percent of whom were Ethiopian nationals and three percent Somali. This highlights Yemen’s ongoing role as a vital transit hub, according to the IOM.

The flow of migrants from the Horn of Africa has persisted into September, showing no sign of stopping despite the recent fighting.

'We come to Yemen, and most Yemenis treat us like brothers'

- Ethiopian migrant

However, the dire humanitarian situation of these African migrants is evident to anyone passing them on city streets, where many sleep outdoors and rely on the charity of passersby for food.

While some find low-wage jobs, the majority depend on the generosity of local Yemenis. Even though more than half of Yemen’s population requires humanitarian assistance, locals still show strong sympathy toward the incoming migrants.

According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (UNOCHA), 22.3 million people in Yemen require some form of humanitarian or protection assistance in 2026.

An Ethiopian migrant working as a cleaner at a shopping mall in Taiz said that he considers Yemen his second home and does not feel like a stranger there.

“We come to Yemen, and most Yemenis treat us like brothers,” he told MEE. “Our goal isn’t to stay here permanently, but to reach Saudi Arabia.”

Acts of giving to the needy

Some restaurants across various governorates, such as Aden and Lahj, distribute free food to people in need - including both Yemenis and African migrants - as the owners view this as an act of charity (sadaqah), an Islamic practice encouraged among believers.

Omar, co-owner of a restaurant in Lahj, distributes food - primarily rice - almost every day to around 40 people in need, including African migrants. He emphasised that they make no distinction between Yemenis and Africans, offering help to anyone who comes to their door.

“Charity does not decrease wealth; rather, it brings blessings to it,” Omar told MEE. “You cannot imagine the happiness of seeing hungry people get a meal. If I could give more, I would not hesitate, as we are acting for the next world, not this one.”

It is not just restaurants that step up; everyday Yemenis are often seen giving food or small cash donations to African migrants out of empathy and a desire to perform acts of charity - an approach Omar believes everyone should embrace.

“You do not need to be a wealthy trader or a restaurant owner to give charity,” Omar said. “Everyone should give based on what they have, as Islam teaches us. We should never judge or treat people based on their nationality.”

Deep historical ties

Ahmed Abdulwahed, who is in his 60s and prefers to be called Uncle Ahmed, confirmed that the positive relationship between Yemen and Ethiopia is ancient, with deep-rooted social ties connecting the two communities.

Uncle Ahmed was born in Ethiopia to an Ethiopian mother and a Yemeni father. He spent more than 20 years there, living out his childhood and youth in the country.

“In times of crisis and difficult economic conditions, some Yemenis would go to Ethiopia in search of work and stability, living there for years before returning to Yemen; conversely, Ethiopians would come to Yemen,” Uncle Ahmed told MEE.

Read More »

He noted that a strong brotherly bond exists, one where a Yemeni never felt like a stranger or merely a temporary resident.

“We lived among the people as if we were one of them, and there was mutual love and respect between Yemenis and Ethiopians,” he added.

“In hard times, each community stood by the other. Yemenis helped their Ethiopian brothers, and Ethiopians likewise stood with Yemenis; thus, the ties between the two were far greater than just a relationship of work or trade.”

Many Yemenis travelled to Ethiopia in the past, and nowadays more are travelling to Djibouti in search of work - especially alongside Yemeni business owners who established enterprises there decades ago.

“There were Yemeni traders and business owners, with some working in various fields such as commerce, the automotive industry, woodworking, and building materials,” Uncle Ahmed added. 

“When I talk about Ethiopia, I am not speaking of a country I passed through briefly, but rather a place where I spent a long period of my life. I have many memories there; life during that time was beautiful and stable, and we lived alongside the people, sharing their joys and sorrows, with social bonds being remarkably strong.”

Uncle Ahmed emphasised that while politics change and circumstances shift, relationships between communities endure.

“Yemenis lived in Ethiopia for many years, and Ethiopians likewise came to Yemen, living and working. Therefore, there is a shared history and social and human ties that political circumstances can never erase,” Uncle Ahmed said.

item.title: Houthi advance on Aden supply route repelled, say Saudi-backed forces
item.description:
Houthi advance on Aden supply route repelled, say Saudi-backed forces

Yemen's Saudi-backed forces said on Thursday that they had repelled overnight attacks by the Houthis on a key supply route to the southern port city of Aden, where the government is based.

The mountain pass known as Hejat al-Abd is a lifeline for forces fighting on behalf of Yemen's Saudi-backed government, which has been hemmed in by a lightning Houthi advance this month linked to the war on Iran.

The road is also critical for goods entering Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city, and its southern and western rural areas, Reuters reported. It is the only route for residents seeking to travel abroad, with no commercial flights operating from Houthi-controlled areas.

The Iran-aligned Houthis have kept up pressure on government forces as they seek to consolidate gains made nearly two weeks ago, when their offensive along Yemen's western coast brought them to the shores of the Red Sea's strategic Bab al-Mandab strait, through which at least ten percent of global maritime trade usually passes.

item.title: A quarter-century after the 'war on terror' began, the American Middle East is over
item.description:
A quarter-century after the 'war on terror' began, the American Middle East is over

Submitted by Hesham Gaafar on Wed, 09/23/2026 - 14:47
The US-built regional order is not collapsing in a single dramatic moment. It is fading quietly into the background - until one day people wake up to an entirely new reality
Antiwar demonstrators hold signs as they gather near the White House in Washington, DC, on 7 April 2026 (Alex Wong/Getty Images/AFP)
Off

Last month, a photographer in Tehran captured a passing scene that seemed unremarkable: people walking past a large anti-American billboard in the city, without so much as glancing up at it. 

The image ran alongside a lengthy essay titled “The End of the American Middle East” by Marc Lynch, a political science professor at George Washington University, in the September/October issue of Foreign Affairs. 

Lynch, who belongs to a critical current within the American academic establishment rather than its fringes, writes that the regional order Washington has sponsored since 1991 has fallen, and that the American-Israeli war with Iran was merely the final bullet in a body that had been bleeding for years.

The question is not whether Lynch is correct - the evidence is difficult to refute - but why it took this long for it to be stated so plainly, in a magazine long seen as a near-official reference point for the American foreign policy establishment. 

What does it mean, for the region’s peoples before their rulers, that an order presented for decades as inescapable fate is now being declared over?

The order that took shape after the 1991 Gulf War rested on two pillars that appeared contradictory, yet worked in tandem. These included dual military containment of Iran and Iraq through bases stretching from the Gulf to the Eastern Mediterranean, and an unwritten bargain with Arab rulers, trading American security guarantees for silence over domestic repression and erasure of the Palestinian question. 

Entire generations of Arabs lived this as daily reality: military aid to rulers who were never questioned about their prisons, a “peace process” renewed every few years without ever approaching a Palestinian state, and an American shield protecting Israel from accountability at the UN Security Council. 

The arrangement never needed popular legitimacy, because it was never built to answer to anyone at home.

Accountability gap

This absence of accountability, which for decades looked like the order’s strength, ultimately became the point of its collapse. A superpower that grants allies unconditional security guarantees exempts them from the price of their own decisions; those who know someone else will bear the consequences take greater risks.

This is what happened in Yemen, where Riyadh found in American backing cover for a war with no clear horizon for victory, sliding the country into catastrophe without a decision-maker paying a political price. 

It happened more dramatically in Gaza, where unconditional American protection became a de facto mandate for an Israeli campaign that has killed more than 73,000 people, many of them women and children. Various international bodies and experts have described it as a genocide. 

An order built on such disregard for public opinion does not need a major crisis to be shaken

The same Washington that mobilised the world to defend Ukraine’s sovereignty simultaneously defended its ally’s right to expand settlements and raze Gaza with impunity - a double standard that deepened the fractures in the perceived legitimacy of the regional order.

That contradiction cost the American system much of its remaining moral authority in the Global South, while the elite consensus sustaining it at home began to crack, amid unprecedented student protests on American campuses and a sharp generational shift in how Americans view Israel. 

When domestic opinion inside the sponsoring state itself questions the bargain, it is no longer just a matter of image abroad, but the start of a rupture in the consensus that lets the bargain continue.

From the outset, American strategy rested on the assumption that ordinary Arab citizens’ opinions carried no real weight, so long as their rulers stayed cooperative - a deeper flaw than any calculation of immediate interest. 

When the 2011 uprisings erupted, demanding bread and dignity, Washington searched less for ways to support democratic transitions, and more for a formula to preserve the existing structure at the lowest cost - a logic that peaked with the Abraham Accords, a security bargain among ruling elites dressed up as historic peace, pushed through without ever reaching a ballot box. 

An order built on such disregard for public opinion does not need a major crisis to be shaken.

Double shock

What distinguished recent years was a double shock: moral, in the collapse of whatever authority Washington claimed following its position on the Gaza holocaust, and military - more painful still for an establishment that defined its regional influence through deterrence.

Despite its devastating campaign against Hezbollah, Israel failed to secure its northern border. The Houthis imposed an effective naval blockade on Israeli-linked Red Sea shipping, withstanding months of American and British strikes - proof that a non-state actor could disrupt global trade against the most formidable military power in history. 

Iran then launched a direct missile barrage towards Israel, shattering a decades-old red line and forcing the American fleet to intervene, highlighting Israel’s dependence on costly US backing. 

In the 2026 war, Washington proved unable even to protect its Gulf allies. The very things that justified the American base network from Qatar to Bahrain - the capacity to deter, guarantee freedom of navigation, and protect allies without direct war - crumbled at once. 

The question now is no longer whether American influence will contract, but how long before that becomes undeniable to everyone.

Lynch invokes the 1956 Suez crisis, the moment Britain and France lost the capacity to impose their will on the region - though both empires needed decades before full withdrawal.

What makes the current moment different is that regional hedging began before the death certificate was written: when Riyadh and Tehran restored relations in 2023 through Chinese mediation that excluded Washington, it signalled regional powers were willing to resolve disputes through other channels. 

Since then, Gulf states have expanded partnerships with Beijing and Moscow, while some joined Brics - insurance against a day when American guarantees no longer demand exclusive loyalty.

Profiting from chaos

The painful irony is that Israel and Iran, the two actors most capable of shaping a new regional order, share an interest in keeping the region on the edge of instability. 

For Israel, a persistent state of war justifies settlement expansion and postpones any reckoning over the state’s treatment of Palestinians. For Tehran, permanent tension offers a ready-made narrative to justify domestic repression - especially after the war left the regime emboldened, having shown it could close the Strait of Hormuz and strike Washington’s allies. 

Caught between them, Washington has no real tools to restrain either - even as it remains, formally, the region’s largest security guarantor.

The war on Iran cracked the US-led regional order. The Mecca pact could deal the final blow
Read More »

The Gulf states, which long wagered that Washington would tip this balance in their favour, now face a painful conclusion: a power that cannot protect its partners from direct attack, nor consult them before a war that reaches them anyway, is no longer the reliable partner the 1991 arrangement was built upon.

The real costs fall not on those who designed the order, but on the peoples never consulted about its shape. Egypt is a stark example: while headlines dwell on missiles and mediation, Cairo bears the direct economic costs of a war it did not choose - fuel and food prices spiking, and Suez Canal revenue collapsing, atop an already deepening financial crisis. These daily bills deserve counting, alongside maps of influence and balances of power.

Lynch closes with a reformist appeal: abandoning military intervention as a first resort, engaging Iran diplomatically instead of isolating it, tying aid to human-rights standards, and accepting a multipolar region that Washington no longer solely defines. This is reasonable in theory, but he never clearly answers who possesses the will to carry it out. 

By his own diagnosis, the current administration is not equipped for a coherent approach of any kind, let alone one requiring real concessions on tools Washington has long treated as axiomatic to its influence. History teaches that institutions abandon entrenched habits only once the costs of continuing exceed the costs of change - which is precisely what appears to be happening now, albeit too slowly for those living through this moment to notice.

This returns us to the image of people walking past that Tehran billboard without a glance - an exact summary of what is happening more broadly. 

The old order is not collapsing in one dramatic moment for all to witness; it is fading slowly into the everyday scenery, until people wake up one morning to a wholly different reality, no longer remembering quite when it began.

item.title: Shipping traffic via Hormuz Strait rises to 10 on Wednesday
item.description:
Shipping traffic via Hormuz Strait rises to 10 on Wednesday

Preliminary shipping data showed 10 commodity vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, increasing from seven a day earlier. 

The traffic still remains below the 10-day moving average of about 17. However, figures are subject to change as some ships switch off their transponders during the voyage.
